analysis.one_liner: Raises corporate tax rates for companies whose CEO pay is more than 50 times their median worker's pay.
analysis.headline: The bill never got past its first step: it was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and received no hearing, markup, or vote before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would raise a company's federal corporate tax rate above the current 21% if its CEO or highest-paid employee earns more than 50 times what its median worker earns. The surcharge is small for ratios just over 50-to-1 (0.5 percentage points) and grows to 5 points for ratios beyond 500-to-1, reaching a 26% top rate. Companies with average annual gross receipts under $100 million are exempt, and the Treasury Secretary must write rules to stop firms from gaming the ratio by swapping employees for contractors.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary workers at large companies with extreme pay gaps, because the tax gives those companies a financial reason to lift median pay or rein in executive compensation, and general taxpayers, because the surcharge raises federal revenue from profitable corporations.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers at large firms with wide pay gaps

how_it_helps.text: Corporations with a pay ratio above 50-to-1 would pay a higher corporate tax rate, starting at 0.5 percentage points and rising in steps to 5 percentage points for ratios above 500-to-1, on top of the current 21% rate.
Companies averaging less than $100 million in annual gross receipts are exempt, so the tax targets only large firms, including large private ones that are not required to file with the SEC.
The bill requires Treasury to write regulations preventing companies from manipulating the ratio, including by replacing employees with contractors.
The pay ratio itself is measured using the disclosure method companies already report to the Securities and Exchange Commission, so no new measurement system would be needed for most covered firms.

analysis.who_pays: Large corporations with the widest CEO-to-worker pay gaps, and their shareholders, who would bear the higher tax; some of the cost could also reach consumers through prices or workers through slower pay growth if firms do not change their pay structures.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large corporations with extreme CEO pay

drawbacks.text: The tax works through an accounting ratio, not directly through wages. A company could respond by raising executive pay even further (pushing the ratio down by raising median pay, but some might instead restructure), by cutting headcount, or by outsourcing work to contractors, and the bill itself acknowledges this contractor risk by ordering anti-avoidance regulations.

A high pay ratio is not always evidence of underpaying workers; some firms employ many low-wage workers by the nature of their business, and the surcharge would tax them for their workforce composition rather than any specific wrongdoing.
The revenue raised is not earmarked for anything in particular; the bill simply increases the corporate rate for certain companies.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The surcharge is modest and graduated, so its direct financial bite is small, but it creates a standing incentive for large companies to narrow the gap between executive and median pay. The main weakness is that it pressures a ratio rather than wages themselves, so a company could comply through restructuring or contractor substitution rather than raising pay, which the bill tries to police through required regulations. It is a targeted, low-rate tax with a real, if indirect, benefit to workers and taxpayers, and an acknowledged risk of avoidance.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never held a hearing, marked it up, or sent it to the floor before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Barbara Lee introduced the bill on January 18, 2024, with 12 initial cosponsors, all Democrats.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day.
No further action — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote — appears in the action history, and the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large corporations with the widest CEO-to-worker pay gaps are better off, since the tax never advanced and no company will owe it. The Ways and Means Committee, which chose not to act, also avoided a floor fight over a corporate tax increase.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High pay-ratio corporations that avoided the tax

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all cosponsors were House Democrats (15 of 216 members of the caucus), no Republican cosponsored, and the Republican-run Ways and Means Committee never moved the bill.

industries.industry: Large corporations with high CEO-to-worker pay ratios (e.g., retail, fast food, tech)
industries.note: These firms would owe a surtax of 0.5 to 5 percentage points on top of the 21% corporate rate unless they narrow the gap between executive and median pay. Their cheapest way to avoid the tax — holding the pay structure as is — is precisely the pay inequality the bill targets, so their interest runs against the workers the bill aims to help.

industries.industry: Small and mid-sized businesses (under $100 million average annual gross receipts)
industries.note: They are exempt from the surcharge, giving them a modest tax advantage relative to the large companies covered by the bill. Ordinary people gain little directly from this carve-out, but it limits the bill's reach to very large firms.

If covered companies shift workers to contractor status to game the ratio, staffing firms could gain business. The bill orders Treasury regulations specifically to prevent this substitution, so any gain depends on evading the rules.
